title: Food for the bereaved
hookLine: make food for the family of Ja'far, for what has come to them (Abu Dawud)

lines: A DISH WITH A NAME ON THE BOTTOM.
cards: A casserole dish with masking tape on the bottom and a name in marker. A tray of rice left on a doorstep. A neighbor who doesn't knock, just texts: it's outside.
Some grieving households end up with a kitchen full of other people's cooking. In Islam, that habit has a sentence behind it, and a name: Ja'far, the Prophet's cousin.
When news of his death reached Madinah, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, didn't give a speech. He gave an instruction about dinner.

teach.b: The hadith is in the Sunan of Abu Dawud, told by Ja'far's son 'Abdullah. The Prophet said, in paraphrase: make food for the family of Ja'far, for something has come to them that keeps them busy. Look at the reason.

Not that they're sad, though they were. That they're occupied. A death takes over a household: the washing, the shroud, the prayer, the burial, the visitors, the phone calls, the children who need explaining to.

Nobody in that house is thinking about lunch, and somebody has to. So the instruction lands on the neighbors, not the family. Jurists later drew a quiet lesson from the same hadith: the burden runs one way.
The neighbors cook for the bereaved household, and the household isn't put to the work and expense of feeding a crowd.

teach.h: A WEEK OF THINGS DONE BY HAND.
teach.b: Now look back over the week. Gentle words at the deathbed. The body washed with care.
Everyone in the same white shroud. The community standing in prayer. The grave, facing the qiblah.
Three days with a door out. And now a pot of food carried across the street. Much of it is done with hands and feet rather than speeches: washing, wrapping, standing, digging, cooking.
In these texts, much of the way through a death is a list of tasks, done for someone who can't do them right now.

how: Muslim neighbors and relatives bring meals to a bereaved household in the first days after a death, following the hadith in Abu Dawud about the family of Ja'far, so the family doesn't have to cook or host.

games.q: what does “food for the bereaved” mean?
o: a meal the grieving family serves to everyone who visits
cooking for a grieving family, because loss keeps them busy
food set out at the grave as an offering for the dead

games.q: food for the bereaved — tap the pairs.
p: for something has come to them

s: the reason given in the hadith is only that the family is sad
the reason given is that something has come to them that keeps them busy.
the instruction is for the neighbors, not the grieving family

the week's practices mostly depend on saying the right words
much of it is done with hands and feet: washing, wrapping, standing, burying, cooking.

games.q: news comes that your neighbor's father has died this morning. what do you do first?
o: wait a week so you don't intrude.
cook something and take it over.
ask them when they'll host the gathering.
games.why: in Abu Dawud, when the news of Ja'far's death came, the Prophet told people to make food for his family.

practice: Bring to mind a household you know that is carrying a loss, this month or this year, and think what they might actually eat: something simple, something that keeps. Picture the dish on their doorstep, left without needing thanks.
If no one comes to mind, let one of the week's words stay with you: soft words, careful hands, white cloth, standing, earth, three days, food.

wordCard.voice: Food for the bereaved. The Prophet's instruction to cook for a grieving family, because what has come to them keeps them busy. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: food, a meal, as given and shared.

carryVoice: Your line: feed the grieving. A pot of rice, left on a step. That's the week, done.
